Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.

revision_notes: A light check surfaced an ITU-sourced figure (via TheGlobalEconomy, fetched and read) of 3.6 kbit/s per internet user for 2016, the last year in a 2012-2016 series, which would correspond to code 1 (Very Low). However a 2019 ITU regional presentation lists Ghana as 'n.a.' for this same indicator, suggesting ITU stopped receiving/publishing this specific metric for Ghana after 2016. A search snippet from ITU DataHub's 'International bandwidth usage' indicator shows a much larger aggregate figure for Ghana (approx. 2.03 million Mbit/s used international bandwidth in 2023), which — if divided by Ghana's approximately 23.4 million internet users in 2023 (69.94% of population per World Bank) — would imply a per-user bandwidth of roughly 87 kbit/s (code 4, Good). This ITU DataHub page is JavaScript-rendered and could not be fetched and read directly to confirm the figure or its unit, so per the rule that a score should not change on a search snippet alone, this manual calculation is not used to set the score. The evidence is contradictory (very low in a stale 2016 point vs a plausible substantial increase implied by an unverified 2023 aggregate), so this is flagged for human review rather than guessed. A human with browser access to datahub.itu.int should confirm the 2023 per-user figure directly.
revised_comments: ITU data (as reported via TheGlobalEconomy) place Ghana's international internet bandwidth at 3.6 kbit/s per internet user in 2016, the most recent year in a 2012-2016 series and well below the global average of around 151 kbit/s per user. More recent ITU DataHub figures point to a substantially larger total volume of used international bandwidth for Ghana by 2023, consistent with the country's subsequent submarine cable landings, but a directly comparable, verified per-user bandwidth estimate for the current period is not available.

revised_source_urls: https://www.purc.com.gh/attachment/547916-20260402040402.pdf (PURC gazetted tariffs, effective 1 April 2026, fetched and read); https://tradingeconomics.com/ghana/gni-per-capita-atlas-method-us-dollar-wb-data.html (World Bank GNI per capita, fetched and read); https://www.bog.gov.gh/economic-data/exchange-rate/ and https://tradingeconomics.com/ghana/currency (Bank of Ghana / market USD-GHS rate, fetched and read)
revision_notes: A light check surfaced a clearly authoritative, current source (PURC, Ghana's electricity regulator), so this was moved to the full path. PURC's gazetted residential tariffs effective 1 April 2026 are: lifeline block (0-30 kWh/month) at GHp86.90/kWh with a GHp213.00/month service charge; 31-300 kWh at GHp196.88/kWh; 301+ kWh at GHp260.15/kWh, plus a GHp1,073.09/month service charge for non-lifeline residential consumers. Ghana's GNI per capita (Atlas method) was US$2,320 in 2024 (World Bank/tradingeconomics), i.e. about US$193/month, and the USD-GHS rate is approximately 11.4 as of July 2026. Applying these figures: a lifeline household (30 kWh) pays roughly US$2.50/month (about 1.3% of monthly GNI per capita — 'Affordable', code 4); a 100 kWh/month household pays roughly US$18/month (about 9.4% — 'Expensive', code 2); a 200 kWh/month household pays roughly US$35/month (about 18% — 'Very Expensive', code 1). Because the resulting code depends heavily on which consumption level is assumed as 'basic', and the metadata does not specify a standard benchmark (unlike, e.g., ESMAP's Multi-Tier Framework, which uses 30/50/100/250 kWh benchmarks), no single code can be asserted with confidence from this data alone. This is flagged for human review with a recommendation to adopt a standard consumption benchmark (e.g. ESMAP's 50 kWh 'Tier 3' benchmark) before scoring.
revised_comments: Ghana's electricity tariffs are set quarterly by the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC). Under tariffs effective 1 April 2026, residential lifeline consumers using up to 30 kWh a month pay GHp86.90 per kWh plus a GHp213.00 monthly service charge, while consumption between 31 and 300 kWh is charged at GHp196.88 per kWh and consumption above 300 kWh at GHp260.15 per kWh, with a higher monthly service charge for non-lifeline consumers. Relative to Ghana's GNI per capita of around US$2,320 (2024) and prevailing exchange rates of roughly GHS11.4 to the US dollar, a household confined to the subsidised lifeline block spends a small share of income on electricity, whereas households consuming above the lifeline threshold face a markedly higher cost burden relative to income.

revision_notes: A light check surfaced a clearly authoritative national source (Ghana Statistical Service), so this was moved to the full path. Ghana's 2021 Population and Housing Census — a full national census, not a sample survey — found that 80.4% of persons aged 6 and above had used an ICT device in the three months before the census, and 68.6% (100% minus the reported 31.4% who had not) had used the internet in the same period; findings were published by GSS in April 2023. This is corroborated by the World Bank/ITU 'individuals using the internet' series, which put Ghana at 69.94% in 2023. Both figures exceed the 60% threshold for the top scale band. An older National Communications Authority/GSS household ICT survey from 2019 (39.7% internet awareness) was also found but is superseded by the more recent and more authoritative census data. Score changed from 0 (Unknown) to 5 (60%+) on the strength of the fetched and read GSS census release and corroborating World Bank data.
revised_comments: Ghana's 2021 Population and Housing Census, published by the Ghana Statistical Service in 2023, found that 80.4% of persons aged six and above had used an ICT device in the three months before the census and 68.6% had used the internet over the same period. This is consistent with World Bank/ITU estimates showing 69.94% of the population using the internet in 2023, indicating that well over 60% of the population has at least basic digital skills.
